subject: English
introduction: Reading comprehension tests your ability to understand, analyze, and interpret written texts. SIMAK passages cover academic, scientific, and social topics. Key skills: identifying the main idea, understanding tone and purpose, making inferences, and finding explicit vs. implicit information.

key_formulas.name: Main idea
key_formulas.formula: \text{What is the passage MOSTLY about? (not a detail)}

key_formulas.name: Inference
key_formulas.formula: \text{What can be CONCLUDED but is NOT directly stated?}

key_formulas.name: Purpose
key_formulas.formula: \text{Why did the author write this? (inform, persuade, describe, warn)}

key_formulas.name: Vocabulary in context
key_formulas.formula: \text{Replace word with synonym; sentence meaning must be preserved}

tips_and_tricks: Read the questions FIRST, then read the passage — you'll know what to look for.
Main idea = what the whole passage is about, NOT what one paragraph says.
For tone questions: look for value-loaded words (impressive, alarming, unfortunately).
Inferences are supported by the text but not stated directly. Eliminate extreme answers.
The correct answer for inference questions is almost never the most obvious or sensational one.
'Best title' should reflect the full passage, not just one section.
Watch for EXCEPT/NOT questions — they require the answer that is NOT supported by the text.

worked_examples.title: Example 1: Identifying main idea
worked_examples.question: A passage describes deforestation, its effects on biodiversity, climate, and local communities, and ends with a call for sustainable policies. What is the main idea?
solution: Step 1: Don't pick a specific detail (e.g., 'deforestation affects birds').
Step 2: The passage covers multiple effects AND a solution → the main idea must be broad.
Step 3: Main idea: 'Deforestation causes serious environmental and social problems that require urgent policy response.'
Key: It covers the scope of the WHOLE passage, not just one paragraph.

worked_examples.title: Example 2: Distinguishing tone
worked_examples.question: In a passage using words like 'alarmingly rapid', 'devastating consequences', and 'urgent action required', what is the author's tone?
solution: Step 3: 'Urgent action required' = calling for immediate response.
Step 4: Tone = concerned/alarmed/urgent (NOT neutral or celebratory).

questions.subject: English
questions.question_text: Which paragraph discusses the historical decline and eventual loss of the library's contents?
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 is dedicated to how the library 'was lost through centuries of neglect, conflict, and fire'.
questions.passage:
The Great Library of Alexandria in Egypt was once the world's largest repository of knowledge, housing hundreds of thousands of papyrus scrolls. Founded in the 3rd century BC, it attracted the greatest scholars of the ancient world. Many (a) ________ texts, from early mathematical proofs to geographical maps, were stored and studied within its massive halls.

Tragically, much of the library was lost through centuries of neglect, conflict, and fire. Historical accounts differ on whether the library was destroyed in a single catastrophic event or through a slow process of decline. However, the result was the same: the permanent loss of countless works by ancient philosophers and scientists, which significantly set back the progress of Western and Middle Eastern thought.

Today, the spirit of the library lives on in projects like the Internet Archive and the new Bibliotheca Alexandrina. These modern initiatives aim to create 'universal libraries' that are accessible to anyone with an internet connection. (1) They use digital preservation to ensure that knowledge is never again lost to physical decay or fire. (2) Most people enjoy reading in the sun. (3) This modern revival emphasizes that global access to information is a fundamental right of humanity.
hints: Consider the main rules of Reading in an English reading context.
Eliminate options that clearly contain grammatical or structural errors.
Paragraph 2 is dedicated to how the library 'was lost through centuries of neglect, conflict, and fire'.

passage_text:
Human memory is not a fixed recording of the past but a dynamic, reconstructive process—one that is far more susceptible to distortion than most people realize. Each time we recall a memory, we do not simply retrieve a stored copy; we actively rebuild it using fragments of the original experience interwoven with our current knowledge, expectations, and emotional state. This reconstructive nature means that memories can change subtly every time they are accessed.

The neuroscience of memory distinguishes between several systems. Declarative memory encompasses facts and events that can be consciously recalled, subdivided into semantic memory (general world knowledge) and episodic memory (autobiographical events). Non-declarative memory, by contrast, operates largely below conscious awareness and includes procedural skills like riding a bicycle. These systems rely on different brain structures: the hippocampus plays a pivotal role in forming new episodic memories, while the cerebellum is central to procedural learning.

Psychologist Elizabeth Loftus spent decades demonstrating how easily false memories can be implanted. In her seminal "lost in the mall" study, approximately 25% of participants came to "remember" a childhood event of being lost in a shopping mall that had never actually occurred, simply after it was described to them by a family member. Her work has had profound implications for the legal system, raising serious questions about the reliability of eyewitness testimony.

These insights challenge the intuitive sense that remembering is passive and neutral. Memory, it turns out, is always a creative act—shaped by who we are at the moment of recall as much as by who we were at the moment of experience.
